Issued at 445 PM CDT Fri Aug 14 2026

-- FORECAST CHANGES OF NOTE/BIG PICTURE COMMENTS/PRIMARY
 UNCERTAINTIES:
- By far the biggest uncertainties involve trying to decipher
  the "exact" details of thunderstorm chances/limited severe
  potential these next few nights. While nothing is "set in
  stone", we at least have "likely" chances/PoPs (60+%) in place
  for portions of our CWA both nights. 

- Latest temperature forecast trends: As has been discussed for
  a few days here, high temps continue to creep upward for 
  Sunday- Monday...with any cooler 70s no longer anticipated. 
  That being said, current indications now point to Wed-Thurs 
  being our next best chance of highs only reaching the 70s...in
  the wake of a cold front tentatively slated for Tuesday 
  night. 

-  Big picture overview of the upper air pattern through the
   next week: As is typical of a summer weather pattern that
   features semi-regular rain chances and temperatures
   reasonably close to "normal" most days, our region will spend
   the entire time along the general interface between a large-
   scale high/ridge centered off to our southeast-through-
   southwest...and the primary upper jet core centered at least
   slightly to our north. However, the spatial orientation of
   our upper flow will evolve from mainly southwesterly these
   next 24 hours (upper high centered over mainly AR/LA/MS)...to
   more zonal/westerly Sun-Tues (as the upper high retrogrades
   back west over the Southern Plains...to finally more
   northwesterly Wed-Fri as the high sets up shop even farther
   west closer to the Four Corners (and a large-scale trough/low
   becomes more established over the eastern United States. 


-- 7-DAY FORECAST CHRONOLOGICAL RUNDOWN (through Fri Aug. 21):
- CURRENT/RECENT WEATHER SCENE AS OF 4 PM: 
In the wake of widespread overnight convection that fortunately
produced very minimal severe weather (but dropped as much as
2-3" of beneficial rain along a narrow axis from roughly Alma-
Hastings), this morning featured lingering-but-gradually-
departing showers, while this afternoon has been dry for the
vast majority of our CWA. Aloft, water vapor imagery and short
term model data clearly reveal a well-defined disturbance
(actually a remnant mesoscale convective vortex/MCV) departing
to our east over IA, while we briefly reside "in between"
disturbances...with the next one gradually approaching out of
CO. 

While skies were mostly cloudy most all areas earlier in the
day, sunshine has gradually become more prevalent in our western
half, while partly/mostly cloudy skies linger longer in our
east. Despite the clouds, the high temperature forecast is at
least mostly on track...with the majority of our Nebraska CWA
realizing highs in the low-mid 80s, and more so upper 80s-low
90s in KS. Our extreme southeastern CWA (mainly Mitchell County
KS) could make a late-day/early evening run at a 100+ heat
index, but this is looking increasingly-unlikely with time).
Winds are very light due to a weak pressure gradient. 


- THIS EVENING-OVERNIGHT:
In short, the next/aforementioned upper wave currently over CO
gradually approaches/invades our CWA...albeit arriving a bit
later than last night's disturbance. As a result, the vast
majority of our CWA likely remains thunderstorm-free through at
least 1 AM (perhaps a few spotty storms try brushing into our
extreme southeast counties such as Mitchell/Jewell/Thayer a bit
earlier in the night?). Beyond 1 AM, higher-res models such as
HRRR (which by the way has been performing quite well the last
few days), brings at least scattered storms...and possibly at
least a small-scale/organized cluster...into our CWA from west-
southwest to east-northeast. Like last night, fairly weak deep
layer shear will be a limiting factor working against much of a
severe threat, but if a cold pool/organized outflow surge can
get going, especially some counties along/south of I-80 could
see a blast of strong to marginally-severe winds...mainly 50-60
MPH, along with perhaps a quick 1-2" of rain. 

Otherwise tonight, low temps similar to last night (mainly mid
60s-low 70s, and winds will remain very light. One thing NOT
currently in our official forecast (but bears watching) is the
possibility for fog development...with the latest HRRR runs
suggesting some fog especially in our far northeastern counties
where any convection/related outflow would be weakest and/or
last to arrive (something to watch).
